items.title: The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron enforced the 1807 ban
items.claim: How was the 1807 abolition of the British slave trade enforced?

options.text: By voluntary compliance from British merchants only

The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron (formed 1808, based at Sierra Leone) intercepted slave ships off the African coast; by the 1860s it had captured around 1,600 ships and freed around 150,000 enslaved Africans
By signing treaties with no enforcement mechanism
By immediately ending all transatlantic shipping

items.reveal:
The West Africa Squadron began with two ships and grew to around 25 by mid-century — about a sixth of the Royal Navy. Captures were brought before Vice-Admiralty courts at Freetown; freed Africans were resettled in Sierra Leone or recruited as 'Liberated African' sailors.

The squadron's mortality rate was very high — yellow fever, malaria, and combat. By the 1840s, treaties with Portugal, Spain and others widened the squadron's powers.

The US South continued importing enslaved people illegally until the Civil War, but the Atlantic trade was largely suppressed by the 1860s. Brazil — the last major importer — banned the trade in 1850 and abolished slavery in 1888.
items.why: Abolishing a trade is different from enforcing the ban. Britain's commitment of naval power for over 60 years made 1807 effective — and reframed the slave trade as an international policing problem.

items.title: Georgian England had 200+ capital offences

options.text: A modernised criminal code that abolished hanging
The expansion of capital crimes from around 50 in 1688 to over 220 by 1815 — including stealing goods worth 12 pence from a shop
A medieval system of trial by ordeal
The system of cattle thieves' execution in Scotland only

items.reveal:
The Waltham Black Act (1723) alone created around 50 new capital offences. Many capital sentences were commuted (juries undervalued goods to avoid death penalty — 'pious perjury'), or replaced by transportation to America (until 1776) and Australia (from 1787).

Reformers — Samuel Romilly, Robert Peel as Home Secretary — gradually reduced the list. By 1841 only treason, murder and a handful of others remained capital. Public hangings at Tyburn ended in 1783 (moved to Newgate); the last public hanging was 1868.
items.why: The Bloody Code shows the early modern state using execution as a substitute for an effective police force. The Victorian shift to imprisonment + policing changes the whole structure of criminal justice.

items.title: Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 CE but converted slowly
items.claim: When did the Roman Empire become Christian?

options.text: Constantine made Christianity the state religion in 312

The Edict of Milan (313) granted religious toleration; Constantine increasingly favoured Christianity but was baptised only on his deathbed in 337; Theodosius I made Christianity the state religion by the Edict of Thessalonica in 380
The empire remained pagan until 600 CE

items.reveal:
Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (28 October 312) over Maxentius came after a reported vision of the Chi-Rho symbol with 'in hoc signo vinces' (in this sign you will conquer). The Edict of Milan, agreed with Licinius in 313, granted religious toleration to all.

Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea (325) and built churches across the empire. He moved the capital to Constantinople (founded 330). He was baptised on his deathbed in 337 by an Arian bishop, Eusebius of Nicomedia.

The Edict of Thessalonica (380) under Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion. Pagan worship was progressively restricted; the Olympic Games were banned in 393.
items.why: Religious change at imperial scale is a process, not a moment. The 67 years between Milan and Thessalonica saw a tolerant empire become a Christian one — a transformation studied by every subsequent religious-political shift.
